mainEntity.name: How long does a try-in appointment usually take?

acceptedAnswer.text: The length of a try-in appointment can vary depending on the complexity of the restoration being assessed. For a single implant crown, the appointment may take around 30–60 minutes. For full-arch restorations involving multiple units, appointments may be longer, particularly if detailed adjustments to the bite or aesthetics are required. Your dental team will give you an indication of expected appointment times as part of your treatment planning. It is worth setting aside sufficient time so that the assessment is not rushed.

mainEntity.name: Can I ask for changes to the tooth colour or shape during a try-in?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — the try-in is specifically designed to be the stage at which such adjustments are discussed and made. If you feel the shade does not match your existing teeth, or if the shape does not feel right, your dental team can communicate these changes to the dental laboratory. Making adjustments at this stage is far simpler than attempting changes after the definitive restoration has been permanently fitted. Honest feedback during the try-in is always encouraged and is a normal part of the process.

mainEntity.name: What happens after the try-in if I am happy with the result?

acceptedAnswer.text: If you and your dental team are satisfied with the fit, function, and aesthetics during the try-in, the information is sent to the dental laboratory to fabricate your final, definitive restoration. Depending on the type of restoration and laboratory turnaround, there may be a waiting period of a few days to a few weeks before the final fitting appointment. Your clinical team will advise you on the expected timeline.

mainEntity.name: Is a try-in always part of implant treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily for every type of restoration or clinical scenario. For straightforward single-unit implant crowns where digital planning and precision are high, some clinicians may proceed directly in certain cases. However, for more complex cases — particularly full-arch implant restorations, cases involving significant aesthetic considerations, or patients with complex bite requirements — a try-in is widely considered an important and valuable stage of treatment. Your dentist will advise on what is appropriate for your individual plan.

mainEntity.name: Can I eat or drink normally with a provisional restoration fitted during a try-in period?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your dental team will give you specific guidance based on your situation. Generally, patients with provisional restorations in place are advised to eat carefully, avoid very hard or sticky foods, and take care not to put excessive force on the temporary restoration. Provisional restorations are not fabricated to the same strength as definitive ones, so some care is sensible during this period. Your dental team will provide tailored advice based on your specific restoration type.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a try-in and a final fitting?

acceptedAnswer.text: A try-in involves placing a provisional or trial version of the restoration to assess fit, bite, and appearance before any permanent decisions are made. Changes can be made at this stage. The final fitting — sometimes called the fit appointment or cementation appointment — is when the definitive, permanent restoration is placed and secured. Once cemented or screwed into place, the restoration is intended to be long-lasting, which is why the try-in stage is so important for ensuring everything is correct beforehand.
